summary:
South Sudan's Penal Code reaches presentation on its face. Section 379 targets "any male person who dresses or is attired in the fashion of a woman" and carries up to three months' imprisonment. For a trans visitor presenting female, that provision is the operative exposure, and it depends on no sexual conduct and no disclosure of identity.

The same code treats consensual same-sex sexual conduct as an "unnatural offense", defined as "carnal intercourse against the order of nature", punishable by up to 10 years' imprisonment. Where the conduct is nonconsensual, the term rises to up to 14 years.

United States State Department country reports on human rights practices covering 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2022 each record that there were no reports of authorities enforcing the same-sex conduct provision. None of those reports describes a repeal, a moratorium or a prosecutorial policy behind that non-enforcement, so the statute stands unrepealed.

Non-enforcement of the text does not equal safety from the state. Those same State Department reports state that security forces routinely harassed LGBTQI+ persons and at times arrested, detained, tortured and beat them between 2018 and 2022, and they describe abuse and discrimination by government agents alongside widespread stigmatisation in the broader population.

Official hostility has been declared in the open. In September 2017 the minister for Labour, Public Service and Human Resource Development, Gathoth Gatkuoth Hothnyang, said the government would order security forces to arrest LGBTQ persons and detain them until they procreate, and no arrests on that basis were reported by the end of that year. The US State Department's 2022 report found that most openly LGBTQI+ citizens had fled South Sudan because of actively hostile government rhetoric and action.

Protective machinery is absent. South Sudan has no hate-crime or anti-discrimination legislation shielding LGBTQ persons from harassment or abuse on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, same-sex couples have no legal recognition, and same-sex marriage has been constitutionally barred since the Constitution was adopted in 2011.

Societal conditions narrow the room further. Stigmatisation is recorded as widespread, and the country has no known LGBTQ-support organisation in operation, leaving a visitor with no local point of contact if something goes wrong.
tangentialFactors:
Security-force violence against LGBTQI+ people is documented across consecutive reporting years rather than in a single incident. The US State Department reports covering 2018 to 2022 record routine harassment and, at times, arrest, detention, torture and beating by security forces, and the same reporting describes abuse and discrimination by government agents.

One episode illustrates how quickly civic space closes. Staff of the LGBTQ-supportive organisation Access for All were detained for several months after a security force raid in 2017 and released without charge, and the organisation was subsequently intimidated into closing; its executive director later left the country.

Rhetoric from the highest levels has hardened visibility risk. Then-President Salva Kiir Mayardit said in July 2010 that homosexuality is not in the "character" of the people of Southern Sudan and would never gain support, while the September 2017 ministerial threat of detention until procreation shows the direction of official intent. A 2006 split in the Episcopal Church of Sudan, in which bishop Abraham Mayom Athiaan left over what he considered insufficient condemnation of homosexuality, marks the same pressure from the religious side.

Displacement functions as the de facto outcome. The US State Department's 2022 report found that most openly LGBTQI+ citizens had left South Sudan because of actively hostile government rhetoric and action, which means visible LGBTQ presence inside the country is already reduced and a standing visitor is more conspicuous for it.

The 2011 State Department report characterised societal discrimination against gay men and lesbians as "widespread", and later reporting does not record a reversal of that finding.
localsOnly:
The Non-Governmental Organisations Act (2016) bars organisations from contravening the country's "sovereignty, ... its institutions and laws". Because same-sex activity is illegal under the Penal Code, that provision may prevent LGBTQ-supportive civic groups from operating at all, and no LGBTQ-support organisation is currently known to be active.

The only anti-discrimination protection on the books is sectoral. As of 2020, harassment of employees based on sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited for all oil and gas companies operating in the country, which leaves employment protection dependent on the employer's industry rather than on general law.

Residents who are visibly gender-nonconforming face Section 379 alongside the social consequences of the wider regime. Openly LGBTQI+ citizens have largely left the country, and those who remain live with the routine harassment, and occasional detention and beating, that the State Department reporting attributes to security forces.

Marriage and partnership provide nothing. Same-sex couples have no legal recognition, and the Constitution adopted in 2011 bars same-sex marriage outright.

Community organising carries personal risk. Access for All was raided by security forces in 2017, its staff were held for several months and released without charge, the organisation was intimidated into closing, and its executive director later departed the country.
outOfScopeNotes:
No sourced material in the inventory addresses entry and visa rules, passport or identity-document gender markers, airport or border screening that could disclose a visitor's trans status, or whether immigration officers apply Section 379 at ports of entry. Those questions remain unresolved here and would need direct verification before travel.

The inventory contains nothing on access to healthcare or transition-related care, on facilities or bathroom rules, or on any hate-crime sentencing enhancement for gender-based violence. Absence of a source is not a finding that these are unrestricted or prohibited.

The non-enforcement record is specific. The US State Department findings for 2018 through 2022 are recorded against the same-sex conduct provision, and the inventory does not establish whether Section 379's gender-presentation offence has ever been charged or enforced, nor the circumstances in which security forces apply it without a charge. That distinction is unresolved.

The inventory does not identify any complaints mechanism, consular protection arrangement or remedy available to a foreign visitor detained under these provisions, and no comparison with neighbouring jurisdictions' laws is sourced.
